The black-and-white image appears to show the unlikeliest of interactions: an orangutan cradling endangered leopard cubs deep in the jungles of Malaysia's Sabah state.

But the viral image is not just unlikely, it is fake, part of a trend of wildlife images generated by artificial intelligence that experts warn endanger animals and people.

Fact-checkers have debunked scores of similar synthetic visuals, from an elephant climbing a tree to escape flooding in Myanmar to a pink dolphin leaping out of water in the Philippines.

They may seem more like feel-good fiction than dangerous misinformation, but experts warn hyper-realistic visuals of wild animals behaving like pets, or even like humans, can distort public perceptions of wildlife and harm conservation efforts.

"This misunderstanding can lead people to approach animals too closely or interact with them in unsafe ways," Jose Guerrero-Casado, a zoology professor at Spain's University of Cordoba, said.

Days after Anthropic announced that text content generated with its Claude AI would include an invisible watermark, the company has released more information about how the marking technology works.

headline: Meta regulates hate speech less in India than globally
body: On Facebook and Instagram, Meta’s proactive enforcement on posts related to hate speech, bullying, harassment, has drastically decreased in India since June 2025
full_body:

In India, only around 30% of posts on Instagram and 32.95% on Facebook promoting hate speech were proactively regulated through Meta’s enforcement directives from October to December 2025. This is in stark contrast to Meta proactively actioning 83.9% of Instagram posts and 74% of Facebook posts related to hateful conduct in the same period globally, according to data from Meta’s Transparency Reports and Community Standards Enforcement Report.

Similar worrying gaps in Meta’s enforcement in India are also prevalent in content promoting bullying, harassment, violence, and incitement. India has Meta’s largest user base in the world.

The degree of Meta’s enforcement on different kinds of posts or accounts which contain content violating community standards - ranging from hate speech, drugs, terror, nudity, sexual activity, child endangerment, and more - is measured through the reported ‘proactive rate’, which is disclosed in its transparency reports. Meta describes this ‘proactive rate’ as “the percentage of all content or accounts acted on” before users report them to Meta.

For example, a proactive rate of 30% for hate speech means that out of all the posts Meta took action on related to hate speech, only 30% of those posts were flagged by Meta before they were reported by users.

The graphic below shows the quarterly proactive rates for different violating pieces of content that Meta actioned on over the years and across Facebook and Instagram, which are also two of the largest social media platforms on the internet. The graphic shows that posts falling under the purview of hate speech/hateful conduct, bullying & harassment, and violence & incitement are proactively actioned on much lesser in India than globally.

This, rather, points to Meta’s reactive moderation relying on user flagging rather than it’s proactive automated scanning and removal of harmful content falling under the above-listed three groups; which is not the case with other forms of harmful content that it proactively moderates (like nudity, child endangerment, terrorism), as shown in the graphic above.
